source.title: Really Strong Features Found in Residual Stream

record.file_problem: The post and comments are present, but the example images and their contents are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports learned residual-stream features and token-ablation examples, but it does not measure whether neurons in the claim's versions are polysemantic or test whether apparently mixed neurons have a shared feature.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern autoencoder features in the residual stream, not the claim's MLP neurons or canonical mixed neurons. Several examples are only headings for unavailable images; rows include only outcomes explicitly stated in the post or comments.
record.test_reason: The post trains a sparse autoencoder (dictionary) on layer-2 residual stream of Pythia-70m and showcases learned features with token-ablation and logit-lens examples. It reports no measurement of neuron polysemanticity (share, cause, architecture dependence, or measurement dependence), so it tests no version. It assumes superposition as motivation for the dictionary method, but does not test it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The author claims the dictionary gives a faithful decomposition (low reconstruction loss, minimal perplexity effect) that could be used to specify traits like honesty. He calls the work 'legit' but preliminary, needing baselines, due diligence and hyperparameter search.
record.recipe_differences: Uses an overcomplete dictionary of learned residual-stream feature directions and token-removal examples; it does not report the original sources' method as a replication.
record.method_sensitivity: The author says different dictionary sizes (1x, 2x, 4x, and 8x residual-stream width) learned progressively more features by the MCS metric; no comparative outcome values are given.

fits_no_version.finding: A sparse dictionary on Pythia-70m layer-2 residual stream yields 3k+ features, mostly single or combined words. Some are context features (Stack Exchange format, Title Case, last name, '[word] and [word]') with intuitive ablation effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse autoencoders on LM residual streams recover interpretable, context-dependent features whose ablation affects predictions in expected ways.

record.problems: The author calls the write-up preliminary and says due diligence and more work are needed. Example images are unavailable in the supplied text, most feature examples therefore cannot be assessed, and no controls or uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The German, One for the Kids, On, and other image-based examples have no readable results in the supplied text. The low-reconstruction-loss/minimal-perplexity statement is not accompanied by a reported measurement, and the dictionary-size/MCS remarks do not give outcome values.

untested.parts: No count of polysemantic MLP neurons. Studies residual-stream autoencoder features.
Superposition is implicitly assumed by the dictionary-learning approach, not tested.
No architecture, activation-function or regularization comparison of neuron polysemanticity.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Uniform binned examples are used, but there is no comparison of how activation range or scoring changes polysemantic classification.

record.verdict_notes: Informal Alignment Forum post. It has no baselines or controls, and most examples were images that are missing from the text. The reader's T6/discusses classification is appropriate. The post does not measure neurons at all, only autoencoder features.

versions.untested_parts: No InceptionV1 or image-classifier neurons are studied.
The post studies learned residual-stream autoencoder features in a small language model, not the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.
No test of superposition or capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of initialization, regularization, or training noise causing polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures, or regularization effects on polysemanticity or performance.
The post does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons to test whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m (actually named 160M!)
rows.operation_detail: Learned dictionary features in the residual stream.
rows.note: The post does not specify which dictionary size produced the 3k+ count; the setup separately says the 4x dictionary has size 2k.
rows.check: Count of dictionary features found, a property of the author's own method. It is not a rate of neuron polysemanticity. It is also ambiguous which dictionary size gave 3k+, given the stated 2k-size 4x dictionary.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m (actually named 160M!)
rows.operation_detail: Removed the Q token from the context and observed the feature activation.
rows.value: Removing Q greatly decreased the feature activation.
rows.locator: Stack Exchange section; author comment on ablated text
rows.note: The author presents this as evidence that the feature detects the Stack Exchange format.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m (actually named 160M!)
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the Title Case feature direction.
rows.note: The post also says the change occurred along with other Title Case texts, without giving additional values.

rows.note: The author adds that last names by themselves are still recognized, but activate the feature less.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m (actually named 160M!)

rows.value: Removing the previous word before "and" has a significant effect some of the time.
rows.note: The author says they are less confident about why the previous word matters and in which contexts.

rows.subject: Pythia-70m (actually named 160M!)
rows.operation_detail: Removed the first word while examining the feature activation.
rows.value: The ablation does not have the expected effect.
rows.locator: Author comment on Beginning & End of First Sentence
rows.note: The author suggests the result may be because removing the first word makes the second word the new first word, and says this was not rigorously studied.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Identified the feature with the highest MCS across multiple layers and model sizes.
rows.value: The highest-MCS feature is described as "beginning & end of first sentence."
rows.note: The author says this feature appears to align with emergent outlier dimensions, but says more work is needed to show this.
rows.check: Subject not stated; 'many layers & model sizes' is unspecified. This is an informal remark about a feature, not a measured outcome. The alignment with outlier dimensions is explicitly unverified.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
